title: Remote State and Locking
intro: A local terraform.tfstate file on your laptop works for one person. The moment a second person or a CI pipeline runs Terraform, you need shared remote state with locking — otherwise two applies can corrupt it.

steps.prompt: You've added an S3 backend block to terraform {} in your config. Initialize and migrate your existing local state into it.
steps.fake_output:
Initializing the backend...
Do you want to copy existing state to the new backend?
  Enter a value: yes

Successfully configured the backend "s3"!
steps.explanation: The local state is copied into S3; from now on every run reads and writes state there.
steps.why: Plain 'terraform init' also detects the backend change and asks to migrate. -migrate-state makes the intent explicit, which matters in scripts. Keep a backup of the old local file until you've confirmed the remote state works.

steps.prompt: Confirm the resources are all still tracked after the migration.
steps.explanation: Same resources as before — now read from S3.
steps.why: If this came back empty, the migration went wrong — and the next plan would try to create everything from scratch, duplicating (or conflicting with) all your live infrastructure.

steps.prompt: You changed the backend's bucket name in config and want to start fresh against it, without migrating anything.
steps.fake_output:
Initializing the backend...
Successfully configured the backend "s3"!
steps.explanation: -reconfigure ignores any previously-saved backend configuration and uses what's in the code now.
steps.why: -migrate-state copies state over; -reconfigure deliberately does NOT. Mixing them up either duplicates state where you didn't want it, or leaves you pointing at an empty backend. Know which one you mean.

steps.prompt: A plan is failing with 'Error acquiring the state lock'. Check the lock ID in the error, then confirm with your team the lock-holder is gone, and release lock 9f2c-44e1.
steps.fake_output:
Do you really want to force-unlock?
  Enter a value: yes

Terraform state has been successfully unlocked!
steps.explanation: Locks prevent two runs from writing state at once. A crashed or killed run can leave a lock behind.
steps.why: force-unlock is only safe when you're CERTAIN no run is still in progress — releasing a lock held by a live apply lets two applies write state simultaneously, which is exactly what corrupts it. Always check first (see terraform-incident-002).
